title: Sirona Menstrual Cups — Safe-Use Decision Card & Size Check (2026)
description: Sizes, silicone, cleaning and IUD cautions from official and regulator sources — plus a safe-use decision card, who should skip a cup and the symptoms that mean seek medical help. Checked 26 Nov 2026.

forWho: Menstruating adults who want to compare a reusable silicone cup with pads or tampons using regulator and peer-reviewed guidance, not brand marketing alone.
Buyers who want a clear first-cycle routine: when to empty, how to sanitise, and when to stop and ask a clinician.
skipIf: Anyone with an IUD, current vaginal infection, recent pregnancy or childbirth, unexplained bleeding or severe period pain should speak to a gynaecologist before using a cup.
Anyone without reliable access to clean water, soap and a way to boil the cup between cycles — cups need washing and sanitising, not a quick wipe.
Anyone with a latex allergy should avoid rubber cups; FDA guidance says choose silicone. We did not verify a batch-specific material certificate for Sirona cups.
Buyers seeking treatment for a medical condition: a menstrual cup is a hygiene product, not a therapy, and this page makes no disease-treatment claims.

content_blocks.heading: Which Sirona cup size, and what are the non-negotiable safety steps?
content_blocks.body: Sirona's official pages describe Small, Medium and Large silicone cups; the older A/B/Teen chart in the static listing was not verified and should not be relied on. FDA guidance says wash hands before and after handling, follow the product instructions, empty typically every 8–12 hours, and boil a reusable cup for one to two minutes at the end of the cycle. Consult a gynaecologist if you have an IUD; stop and seek care for itching, rash, pain, swelling or TSS symptoms. Durza did not handle, insert or test any cup.

items.title: First cycle: plan to change more often than the maximum
items.body: FDA guidance says a cup is typically removed and emptied every 8 to 12 hours, and that users should follow their product's instructions. Sirona's indexed pages advertise up to 8 hours of protection. For a first cycle, treat the shorter end as the planning number until you know your flow and fit — do not aim for the longest advertised interval.

items.title: Size: trust the current chart on the pack, not an old chart
items.body: Indexed Sirona pages describe three sizes — Small for teens / under-30s who have not given birth, Medium for most users, Large for those who have given birth or have heavier flow. The static Durza entry's A/B/Teen table could not be confirmed on the official site and is not repeated here. If you are between sizes, use the manufacturer's current size chart and ask a clinician rather than guessing.

items.title: Cleaning is the real cost of a reusable cup
items.body: FDA says wash the cup with soap and water before insertion, wash it again after emptying, and at the end of the cycle wash and place it in boiling water for one to two minutes. CDC gives the same boil-for-one-to-two-minutes instruction. If you cannot do this privately and reliably, a disposable product may be the safer practical choice.

items.title: IUD, infection, pregnancy: get individual advice
items.body: FDA states cups may interfere with IUD strings and placement and advises consulting a gynaecologist; a systematic review of seven publications reported IUD expulsion rates of 3.7%, 17.3% and 18.6% in some series, with causation uncertain. FDA also says cups are not intended for non-period bleeding such as from current infection or recent pregnancy/childbirth.

items.title: What the evidence does and does not show
items.body: A 2019 Lancet Public Health review of 43 studies and 3,319 participants found cups to be a safe option with leakage comparable to pads or tampons, while noting that good-quality studies were limited. This supports cups as a hygiene option; it does not prove any brand-specific benefit or any health outcome Durza did not measure.

items.body: Choose size from the current official size chart, not from a generic age chart; if you have an IUD or recently gave birth, ask a clinician first.
Confirm the material marked on the pack. FDA advises silicone for anyone sensitive to latex; Durza has not verified a batch-specific material certificate.
Decide whether you can wash hands, rinse the cup and boil it at cycle end. If not, buy a disposable option instead.
At checkout, test any code in the cart. CUPFREE and SIRONA15 come from an older Durza draft and were not verified on 26 Nov 2026 — do not treat them as active.
On arrival, follow the manufacturer's first-use cleaning instructions before insertion and keep the instructions for reference.

items.label: FDA: empty typically every 8–12 hours; boil at cycle end
items.value: FDA's menstrual-cup page says to wash hands before and after handling, wash the cup with soap and water per instructions, remove and empty it typically every 8 to 12 hours, and at the end of the cycle wash it and place it in boiling water for one to two minutes.

items.label: CDC gives the same one-to-two-minute boil instruction
items.value: CDC's menstrual hygiene guidance says to clean cups every day after use and to sanitise after the period by rinsing thoroughly and boiling for one to two minutes. It also advises washing hands before and after using any menstrual product.

items.label: IUD users should consult a gynaecologist
items.value: FDA states cups could interfere with IUD strings and placement and advises consulting a gynaecologist. A systematic review of cup use with IUDs reported expulsion rates of 3.7%–18.6% in some included publications; studies differed on whether the cup caused it.

items.label: The 2019 systematic review found cups a safe option
items.value: The Lancet Public Health review pooled 43 studies with 3,319 participants and reported cup leakage comparable to pads or tampons, with adverse events generally rare; the authors called for better-quality studies. Durza did not run a clinical study.

items.label: Stop use and seek care for local symptoms
items.value: FDA advises stopping cup use and contacting a healthcare provider if you experience itching, rash, pain, swelling or discomfort. Its tampon page lists TSS warning signs — sudden high fever, chills, nausea or vomiting, diarrhoea, rash, dizziness or fainting, low blood pressure — and says to seek emergency care if they occur.

items.label: Sirona's own page claims are brand-stated
items.value: Indexed Sirona pages describe 100% medical-grade silicone, Small/Medium/Large sizes, up to 8 hours of protection and reuse up to five years, and use the phrase 'FDA-approved'. Durza's direct fetch was rate-limited, we saw no batch certificate, and we do not verify the FDA-approval wording.

content_blocks.text: We checked FDA and CDC menstrual-product guidance, the 2019 Lancet Public Health systematic review, an IUD/cup systematic review and indexed Sirona product pages on 26 Nov 2026. Sirona's pages were rate-limited, so brand statements are quoted from search snippets and not independently verified. Durza did not purchase, handle, insert, sterilise or test any cup and makes no medical claim. Durza earns a commission on qualifying purchases through tracked links at no extra cost to you.

items: Original contribution — safe-use decision card: (1) menstruating only; (2) wash hands; (3) wash cup with soap and water before insertion; (4) empty on schedule, at the short end while learning; (5) rinse and wash before reinserting; (6) boil one to two minutes after the cycle; (7) stop for itching, rash, pain, swelling or unusual discharge; (8) consult a gynaecologist first with an IUD, infection, recent pregnancy/childbirth or unexplained pain.

Seek urgent medical help for sudden high fever, vomiting or diarrhoea, rash, dizziness/fainting or confusion — possible TSS signs per FDA/MedlinePlus — especially if a cup has been left in longer than instructed.

The old Durza chart using A/B/Teen sizes and the claim that 'virgins under 18' should use tampons or pads were not verified; size and suitability should come from the current manufacturer chart and, where relevant, a clinician.
Cup use does not treat heavy bleeding, pain, infection or any disease; persistent heavy flow, severe pain or unusual odour needs medical assessment.
No coupon code is claimed as active. CUPFREE and SIRONA15 were not verified on the live site on 26 Nov 2026.

items.q: Which Sirona size should I buy?
items.a: Indexed Sirona pages describe Small, Medium and Large, with Small positioned for teens/under-30s who have not given birth and Large for heavier flow or after childbirth. The older Durza A/B/Teen chart was not verified and is not relied on. Use the current size chart on the product page and ask a clinician if you are unsure.

items.q: How long can a menstrual cup stay in?
items.a: FDA says cups are typically emptied every 8 to 12 hours and that you should follow the product instructions. Sirona's indexed pages claim up to 8 hours. Plan shorter intervals during your first cycles rather than stretching to the maximum.

items.q: Can I use a cup with an IUD?
items.a: Possibly, but FDA advises consulting a gynaecologist because cups may interfere with IUD strings and placement. Published series report IUD expulsion among cup users, though studies disagree about causation. Get individual advice.

items.q: How do I clean it between cycles?
items.a: FDA and CDC both say to wash the reusable cup with soap and water and then boil it for one to two minutes at the end of the cycle. Wash hands before and after handling, and wash the cup after each emptying before reinserting.

items.q: What symptoms mean I should stop and get help?
items.a: Stop using the cup and contact a healthcare provider for itching, rash, pain, swelling or discomfort. Seek urgent care for sudden high fever, chills, vomiting/diarrhoea, rash, dizziness or fainting — possible TSS warning signs.

items.q: Did Durza test the cup or verify 'FDA-approved'?
items.a: No. We did not purchase or handle a cup, and the Sirona product page was rate-limited during this check. The 'FDA-approved' wording appears in brand snippets only; we do not verify a specific clearance or a batch certificate.
